result.statement: On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given finite straight line. It is required to construct an equilateral triangle on AB.

**Step 2.** With centre A and distance AB, describe the circle BCD. [P3]

**Step 3.** With centre B and distance BA, describe the circle ACE. [P3]

**Step 4.** Let C be a point at which the two circles cut one another. Draw the straight lines CA and CB from the point C to the points A and B. [P1]

**Step 5.** Since the point A is the centre of the circle CDB, and the straight lines AC and AB are drawn from A to the circumference, AC is equal to AB. [D1.15]

**Step 6.** Since the point B is the centre of the circle CAE, and the straight lines BC and BA are drawn from B to the circumference, BC is equal to BA. [D1.15]

**Step 7.** Therefore each of the straight lines CA and CB is equal to AB. Things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another; therefore CA is equal to CB. [CN1]

**Step 8.** Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, and BC are equal to one another. Hence the triangle ABC has its three sides equal and is therefore equilateral. [D1.20]

**Step 9.** Thus the equilateral triangle ABC has been constructed on the given finite straight line AB, which was required to be done.

result.statement: To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given point and BC the given straight line. It is required to place at the point A a straight line equal to BC.

**Step 2.** Join the straight line AB from the point A to the point B [P1].

**Step 3.** On AB construct the equilateral triangle DAB [1.1].

**Step 4.** Produce the finite straight lines DA and DB in a straight line to E and F respectively [P2].

**Step 5.** With centre B and distance BC describe the circle CGH, and let it meet DF (produced) at the point G [P3].

**Step 6.** With centre D and distance DG describe the circle GKL, and let it meet DE (produced) at the point L [P3].

**Step 7.** Since the point B is the centre of the circle CGH, and BC and BG are straight lines falling upon the circle from the centre, BC is equal to BG [D1.15].

**Step 8.** Since the point D is the centre of the circle GKL, and DL and DG are straight lines falling upon the circle from the centre, DL is equal to DG [D1.15].

**Step 9.** Since the triangle DAB is equilateral, its sides DA and DB are equal to one another [D1.20].

**Step 10.** From the equals DL and DG (Step 8) subtract the equals DA and DB (Step 9); the remainders AL and BG are then equal [CN3].

**Step 11.** BC was shown equal to BG (Step 7), and AL is also equal to BG (Step 10); therefore, being equal to the same thing BG, AL and BC are equal to one another [CN1].

**Step 12.** Therefore at the given point A the straight line AL has been placed equal to the given straight line BC, which was required to be done.

result.statement: Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the less.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB and C be the two given unequal straight lines, of which AB is the greater. It is required to cut off from AB, the greater, a straight line equal to C, the less.

**Step 2.** At the point A, place the straight line AD equal to the straight line C [1.2].

**Step 3.** With centre A and distance AD, describe the circle DEF [P3]. Since AB is greater than C, and C is equal to AD, the point B lies beyond the circumference, so the circle meets AB at a point E lying between A and B.

**Step 4.** Since the point A is the centre of the circle DEF, and AD and AE are both straight lines drawn from the centre to the circumference, AE is equal to AD [D1.15].

**Step 5.** But C is also equal to AD (Step 2). Therefore each of the straight lines AE and C is equal to AD; hence AE is equal to C [CN1].

**Step 6.** Therefore, given the two straight lines AB and C, from AB the greater, the straight line AE has been cut off equal to C the less. Q.E.F.

result.statement: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and having the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF. We must show that the base BC is equal to the base EF, that the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF, and that the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend: the angle ABC to the angle DEF, and the angle ACB to the angle DFE.

**Step 2.** Apply the triangle ABC to the triangle DEF so that the point A is placed on the point D and the straight line AB is placed along the straight line DE. Since AB is equal to DE, the point B will coincide with the point E, for the two equal straight lines AB and DE laid out from the same point D in the same direction reach the same point.

**Step 3.** Since AB now lies along DE, and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF, the straight line AC will fall along the straight line DF; for the inclination of AC to AB is the same as the inclination of DF to DE, so that AC, laid off from D on the same side of DE as DF, takes the same direction as DF.

**Step 4.** Since AC is equal to DF, the point C will coincide with the point F, for the two equal straight lines AC and DF laid out from the same point D along the same straight line reach the same point.

**Step 5.** Now B coincides with E and C coincides with F. The base BC is the straight line joining B to C, and the base EF is the straight line joining E to F; by P1 the straight line joining two given points is a determinate straight line, so that there is only one straight line from E to F. If BC did not coincide with EF while B lay on E and C on F, two distinct straight lines would join the same two points E and F and would enclose a space, which is impossible. Therefore the base BC coincides with the base EF.

**Step 6.** Since the base BC coincides with the base EF, the base BC is equal to the base EF (CN4).

**Step 7.** Since the point A coincides with D, B with E, and C with F, and the sides AB, AC, BC coincide with the sides DE, DF, EF respectively, the whole triangle ABC coincides with the whole triangle DEF; therefore the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF (CN4).

**Step 8.** Likewise, the side BA coincides with ED and the side BC with EF, so the angle ABC, contained by BA and BC, coincides with the angle DEF, contained by ED and EF; therefore the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF (CN4). And the side CA coincides with FD and the side CB with FE, so the angle ACB coincides with the angle DFE; therefore the angle ACB is equal to the angle DFE (CN4).

**Step 9.** Thus the base BC is equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely the angle ABC (subtended by AC) to the angle DEF (subtended by DF), and the angle ACB (subtended by AB) to the angle DFE (subtended by DE). This is what was to be proved.

**USED:** P1, CN4

result.statement: In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be an isosceles triangle having the side AB equal to the side AC (D1.20). Produce the straight lines AB and AC further in a straight line to D and E respectively (P2). I say that the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, and the angle CBD to the angle BCE.

**Step 2.** Let a point F be taken at random on BD. Since a finite straight line may be produced continuously as far as required (P2), let AE be taken greater than AF; from AE the greater cut off AG equal to AF the less (1.3). Join the straight lines FC and GB (P1).

**Step 3.** Since AF is equal to AG and AB to AC, the two sides FA, AC are equal to the two sides GA, AB respectively, and they contain a common angle, the angle FAG. Therefore, in the triangles AFC and AGB, the base FC is equal to the base GB, the triangle AFC is equal to the triangle AGB, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend: the angle ACF is equal to the angle ABG, and the angle AFC is equal to the angle AGB (1.4).

**Step 4.** Since the whole AF is equal to the whole AG, and in these AB is equal to AC, the remainder BF is equal to the remainder CG (CN3).

**Step 5.** But FC was also proved equal to GB; therefore the two sides BF, FC are equal to the two sides CG, GB respectively. And the angle BFC is equal to the angle CGB, for since B lies on AF and C lies on AG, these are the very angles AFC and AGB which were shown equal in Step 3. The base BC is common to the two triangles BFC and CGB. Therefore the triangle BFC is equal to the triangle CGB, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend: the angle FBC is equal to the angle GCB, and the angle BCF is equal to the angle CBG (1.4).

**Step 6.** Since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the whole angle ACF (Step 3), and in these the angle CBG is equal to the angle BCF (Step 5), the remaining angle ABC is equal to the remaining angle ACB (CN3); and these are at the base of the triangle ABC.

**Step 7.** The angle FBC was also proved equal to the angle GCB (Step 5); and since F lies on BD and G lies on CE, these are the angles DBC and ECB, which are under the base. Therefore in isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another. Q.E.D.

**USED:** D1.20, P1, P2, 1.3, 1.4, CN3

result.statement: If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB. I say that the side AB, which subtends the angle ACB, is equal to the side AC, which subtends the angle ABC.

**Step 2.** Suppose AB is not equal to AC. Then one of them is greater; let AB be the greater.

**Step 3.** Since AB is greater than AC, cut off from AB (the greater) a straight line DB equal to AC (the less), with D lying on AB between A and B [1.3].

**Step 4.** Join the straight line DC [P1].

**Step 5.** In the triangles DBC and ACB: DB is equal to AC (Step 3), and BC is common to both, so the two sides DB, BC are equal to the two sides AC, CB respectively.

**Step 6.** Moreover, the angle DBC contained by DB, BC is the same as the angle ABC, since D lies on AB; and by hypothesis the angle ABC is equal to the angle ACB, which is contained by AC, CB. Hence the angles contained by the equal sides are equal.

**Step 7.** Therefore, two sides of triangle DBC being equal to two sides of triangle ACB respectively, and the contained angles being equal, the base DC is equal to the base AB, and the triangle DBC is equal to the triangle ACB [1.4].

**Step 8.** But the triangle DBC is a part of the triangle ACB, since D lies on the side AB between A and B; and the whole is greater than the part [CN5]. Thus the less triangle would be equal to the greater, which is absurd.

**Step 9.** Therefore the supposition that AB is unequal to AC is impossible; by the same argument, AC cannot be greater than AB. Hence AB is equal to AC.

**Step 10.** Therefore, if in a triangle two angles are equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles are also equal to one another. Q.E.D.

result.statement: Given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a point, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AC, CB be the two straight lines constructed on the straight line AB from its extremities A, B and meeting at the point C. Suppose, if possible, that two other straight lines AD, DB are constructed on AB from A, B, on the same side of AB as C, meeting at a point D different from C, and equal to the former two respectively, each to that which has the same extremity with it: AD = AC and DB = CB. Join CD (P1).

**Step 2.** Since AC = AD, the angles at the base CD of triangle ACD are equal: ∠ACD = ∠ADC (1.5). Since CB = DB, the angles at the base CD of triangle CBD are equal: ∠DCB = ∠CDB (1.5).

**Step 3.** Because D lies on the same side of AB as C and D ≠ C, at least one of the following holds: (I) D lies on neither of the straight lines AC, CB, and neither of the points C, D lies within the triangle formed by AB with the other point; (II) one of C, D lies within the triangle formed by AB with the other; (III) D lies on AC or on CB. The hypothesis is unchanged by interchanging A with B, and by interchanging C with D; so in (II) we may take D within triangle ACB, and in (III) we may take D on AC.

**Step 4 (Case I).** By the symmetry in A and B, let D and A lie on opposite sides of CB. Then D and B lie on the same side of CA (otherwise C would be within triangle ADB); A and B lie on the same side of CD (otherwise CD would cut AB at a point M between A and B, and since C, D are on the same side of AB, M would lie on CD produced beyond C or beyond D, so that C would be within triangle ADB or D within triangle ACB); and A and C lie on the same side of DB (since CB falls between BA and BD). Consequently CB falls within the angle ACD, and DA falls within the angle CDB.

**Step 5.** Since CB falls within ∠ACD, the angle DCB is a part of the angle ACD; therefore ∠ACD > ∠DCB (CN5). But ∠ADC = ∠ACD (Step 2); therefore ∠ADC > ∠DCB.

**Step 6.** Since DA falls within ∠CDB, the angle ADC is a part of the angle CDB; therefore ∠CDB > ∠ADC (CN5). Combined with Step 5, ∠CDB is much greater than ∠DCB.

**Step 7.** But ∠CDB = ∠DCB (Step 2). Thus ∠CDB is both equal to and greater than ∠DCB, which is impossible. Case I cannot occur.

**Step 8 (Case II).** Let D lie within triangle ACB. Produce AC beyond C to E, and AD beyond D to F (P2). Since AC = AD, the angles under the base CD of triangle ACD are equal: ∠DCE = ∠CDF (1.5).

**Step 9.** Since D lies within the angle ACB, CB falls between CD and CE; so the angle DCB is a part of the angle DCE, and ∠DCE > ∠DCB (CN5).

**Step 10.** Since D lies within triangle ACB, AD produced beyond D meets CB at a point between C and B; so DF falls within the angle CDB, the angle CDF is a part of the angle CDB, and ∠CDB > ∠CDF (CN5). Hence ∠CDB > ∠CDF = ∠DCE > ∠DCB, that is, ∠CDB > ∠DCB.

**Step 11.** But ∠CDB = ∠DCB (Step 2), which is impossible. Case II cannot occur.

**Step 12 (Case III).** Let D lie on the straight line AC. Since D is on the same side of AB as C, D lies on AC itself or on AC produced beyond C; and since D ≠ C, either AD is a part of AC or AC is a part of AD. Hence AD and AC are unequal (CN5), contrary to the hypothesis AD = AC. Case III cannot occur.

**Step 13.** Each possible position of D leads to an impossibility. Therefore there cannot be constructed on AB, from its extremities and on the same side of it, two other straight lines AD, DB meeting in a point D other than C and equal respectively to AC, CB, each to that which has the same extremity with it. Q.E.D.

Path note: Case I (Steps 4–7) is the direct route via the base angles of the two isosceles triangles and whole-greater-than-part; Cases II and III are included only to make the position analysis exhaustive, and Case II is the sole reason P2 is invoked.

result.statement: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and let them also have the base BC equal to the base EF. I say that the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 2.** Apply the triangle ABC to the triangle DEF so that the point B is placed on the point E and the straight line BC on the straight line EF, with the vertex A falling on the same side of EF as D. Since BC is equal to EF, the point C will also coincide with the point F, so that the base BC coincides with the base EF.

**Step 3.** I say that the sides BA, AC will then also coincide with the sides ED, DF. For suppose, the base BC coinciding with the base EF, that the sides BA, AC do not coincide with ED, DF but fall beside them, as EG, GF, meeting at some point G different from D. Then on the straight line EF, from its extremities E, F, there have been constructed the two straight lines ED, DF meeting at the point D; and on the same straight line EF, from the same extremities E, F, and on the same side of it, there have been constructed two other straight lines EG, GF meeting at another point G, and these are equal to the former two respectively, each to that which has the same extremity with it: for EG is the side BA, which is equal to ED, and GF is the side AC, which is equal to DF.

**Step 4.** But two such straight lines cannot be constructed on the same straight line, from its extremities, on the same side, meeting at a different point and equal respectively to the former two [1.7]. Therefore it is impossible that, when the base BC is applied to the base EF, the sides BA, AC should fail to coincide with ED, DF; hence they coincide with them.

**Step 5.** Since the sides BA, AC coincide with the sides ED, DF, the angle BAC contained by BA, AC coincides with the angle EDF contained by ED, DF, and things which coincide with one another are equal to one another [CN4]. Therefore the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 6.** Therefore, if two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To bisect a given rectilineal angle.
result.proof:
## Proposition 1.9
**Statement:** To bisect a given rectilineal angle.

**Step 1.** Let the angle BAC be the given rectilineal angle, contained by the two straight lines AB and AC. It is required to bisect it.

**Step 2.** Let a point D be taken at random on AB.

**Step 3.** From AC let AE be cut off equal to AD [1.3].

**Step 4.** Let DE be joined [P1].

**Step 5.** On DE let the equilateral triangle DEF be constructed, on the side of DE remote from A [1.1].

**Step 6.** Let AF be joined [P1].

**Step 7.** Since the triangle DEF is equilateral, the side DF is equal to the side EF [D1.20].

**Step 8.** Now, since AD is equal to AE (Step 3) and AF is common, the two sides DA, AF are equal to the two sides EA, AF respectively; and the base DF is equal to the base EF (Step 7).

**Step 9.** Therefore the angle DAF is equal to the angle EAF [1.8].

**Step 10.** Therefore the given rectilineal angle BAC has been bisected by the straight line AF. Q.E.F.

**USED:** P1, D1.20, 1.1, 1.3, 1.8

result.statement: To bisect a given finite straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given finite straight line. On AB construct the equilateral triangle ABC [1.1].

**Step 2.** Since triangle ABC is equilateral, its three sides are equal to one another; in particular, AC is equal to CB [D1.20].

**Step 3.** Bisect the rectilineal angle ACB by the straight line CD, where D is the point in which the bisecting line meets AB [1.9]. Then the angle ACD is equal to the angle BCD.

**Step 4.** Consider the triangles ACD and BCD. The side AC is equal to the side CB (Step 2), the side CD is common to both triangles, and the angle ACD contained by AC, CD is equal to the angle BCD contained by CB, CD (Step 3). Therefore the two sides AC, CD are equal to the two sides BC, CD respectively, and the contained angles are equal; hence the base AD is equal to the base DB [1.4].

**Step 5.** Therefore the given finite straight line AB has been bisected at the point D. Q.E.F.

result.statement: To draw a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point on it.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line and C the given point on it. It is required to draw from the point C a straight line at right angles to AB.

**Step 2.** Let a point D be taken at random on AC. From CB cut off CE equal to CD [1.3]. (Should CB be less than CD, first produce AB continuously beyond B [P2] so that the part of the line on the side of B exceeds CD; 1.3 then cuts off CE from that greater part.) Thus D, C, E lie on the one straight line AB (or AB produced), with C between D and E, and DC = CE.

**Step 3.** On DE construct the equilateral triangle FDE [1.1], and join FC [P1].

**Step 4.** Since the triangle FDE is equilateral, its side DF is equal to its side FE [D1.20].

**Step 5.** Consider the triangles DCF and ECF. Since DC = CE (Step 2) and CF is common, the two sides DC, CF are equal to the two sides EC, CF respectively; and the base DF is equal to the base FE (Step 4). Therefore the angle DCF, contained by the equal sides DC, CF, is equal to the angle ECF, contained by the equal sides EC, CF [1.8].

**Step 6.** The angles DCF and ECF are adjacent angles, made by the straight line CF set up on the straight line DE (which is AB). When a straight line set up on a straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is right, and the straight line standing on the other is called a perpendicular to it [D1.10]. Therefore each of the angles DCF, FCE is right, and CF is perpendicular to AB.

**Step 7.** Therefore the straight line CF has been drawn at right angles to the given straight line AB from the given point C on it. Q.E.F.

**USED:** P1, P2, D1.10, D1.20, 1.1, 1.3, 1.8

result.statement: To a given infinite straight line, from a given point which is not on it, to draw a perpendicular straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given infinite straight line and C the given point which is not on it. It is required to draw from the point C a straight line perpendicular to AB.

**Step 2.** Take a point D at random on the other side of the straight line AB from C.

**Step 3.** With centre C and distance CD, describe the circle EFG [P3]. Since C lies on one side of AB and D on the other, the circumference of this circle crosses AB; let it cut AB at the two points E and G.

**Step 4.** Bisect the straight line EG at the point H [1.10].

**Step 5.** Join the straight lines CG, CH, CE [P1].

**Step 6.** Since EG has been bisected at H, GH is equal to HE.

**Step 7.** HC is common to the two triangles CHG and CHE.

**Step 8.** Since C is the centre of the circle EFG and the points G and E lie on its circumference, CG is equal to CE [D1.15].

**Step 9.** Therefore in the triangles CHG and CHE the two sides GH, HC are equal to the two sides EH, HC respectively, and the base CG is equal to the base CE. Hence the angle CHG is equal to the angle EHC [1.8].

**Step 10.** The angles CHG and EHC are adjacent angles, made by the straight line CH set up on the straight line AB. When a straight line set up on a straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is right, and the straight line standing on the other is called a perpendicular to that on which it stands [D1.10].

**Step 11.** Therefore CH has been drawn from the given point C, which is not on AB, perpendicular to the given infinite straight line AB. Q.E.F.

result.statement: If a straight line set up on a straight line make angles, it will make either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let any straight line AB set up on the straight line CD make the angles CBA and ABD. I say that either the angles CBA, ABD are two right angles, or that together they are equal to two right angles.

**Step 2.** First, suppose the angle CBA is equal to the angle ABD. Then the straight line AB set up on the straight line CD makes the adjacent angles equal to one another; hence each of the angles CBA, ABD is a right angle (D1.10). Therefore the two angles are two right angles, and the proposition holds in this case.

**Step 3.** Next, suppose the angle CBA is not equal to the angle ABD. From the point B on the straight line CD draw the straight line BE at right angles to CD (1.11). Then, since BE set up on CD makes the adjacent angles CBE, EBD equal to one another, each of them is a right angle (D1.10); so the angles CBE, EBD are two right angles.

**Step 4.** Since the angles CBA, ABD are unequal, AB does not coincide with BE, and so BE falls within one of the two angles CBA, ABD. Without loss of generality, let BE fall within the angle CBA, so that the angle CBE is made up of the two angles CBA and ABE, and the angle DBA is made up of the two angles DBE and EBA.

**Step 5.** Since the angle CBE is equal to the two angles CBA, ABE taken together, let the angle EBD be added to each. Then the angles CBE, EBD taken together are equal to the three angles CBA, ABE, EBD taken together (CN2).

**Step 6.** Again, since the angle DBA is equal to the two angles DBE, EBA taken together, let the angle ABC be added to each. Then the angles DBA, ABC taken together are equal to the three angles DBE, EBA, ABC taken together (CN2).

**Step 7.** But the angles CBE, EBD were shown in Step 5 to be equal to the same three angles. Things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another (CN1); therefore the angles CBE, EBD taken together are equal to the angles DBA, ABC taken together.

**Step 8.** But the angles CBE, EBD are two right angles (Step 3). Therefore the angles DBA, ABC taken together are equal to two right angles.

**Step 9.** Hence, in either case, the straight line AB set up on the straight line CD makes either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles. Therefore, if a straight line set up on a straight line make angles, it will make either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles. Q.E.D.

**USED:** D1.10, 1.11, CN2, CN1

result.statement: If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight line with one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be any straight line and B a point on it, and let BC, BD be two straight lines not lying on the same side of AB, such that at the point B the adjacent angles ABC, ABD together are equal to two right angles. I say that BD is in a straight line with CB.

**Step 2.** Suppose that BD is not in a straight line with BC. Produce the finite straight line CB in a straight line to a point E, so that CBE is one straight line [P2]. Since BD and BE both lie on the side of AB opposite to C, and BE is a different line from BD, the angle ABE and the angle ABD are unequal, one being a part of the other.

**Step 3.** Since the straight line AB is set up on the straight line CBE, the angles ABC, ABE are equal to two right angles [1.13].

**Step 4.** But by hypothesis the angles ABC, ABD are also equal to two right angles. Since all right angles are equal to one another [P4], the two right angles in Step 3 and the two right angles of the hypothesis are the same magnitude; hence the angles ABC, ABE together are equal to the angles ABC, ABD together, being each equal to two right angles [CN1].

**Step 5.** Let the common angle ABC be subtracted from each; then the remaining angle ABE is equal to the remaining angle ABD [CN3].

**Step 6.** But by Step 2 one of the angles ABE, ABD is a part of the other, so the less would be equal to the greater, which is impossible, since the whole is greater than the part [CN5].

**Step 7.** Therefore BE is not in a straight line with CB. In the same way it can be shown that no straight line other than BD can be in a straight line with CB, for any such line would give the same contradiction. Therefore CB is in a straight line with BD, which was to be proved.

**USED:** P2, P4, CN1, CN3, CN5, 1.13

result.statement: If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the two straight lines AB and CD cut one another at the point E. We must show that the vertical angles are equal: angle AEC is equal to angle DEB, and angle CEB is equal to angle AED.

**Step 2.** The straight line AE stands upon the straight line CD and makes with it the adjacent angles CEA and AED. Therefore, by 1.13, the angles CEA and AED are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 3.** Again, the straight line DE stands upon the straight line AB and makes with it the adjacent angles AED and DEB. Therefore, by 1.13, the angles AED and DEB are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 4.** By P4, all right angles are equal to one another, so two right angles constitute one and the same magnitude wherever they occur. Hence the angles CEA, AED together and the angles AED, DEB together are each equal to the same thing, namely two right angles; therefore, by CN1, the angles CEA, AED together are equal to the angles AED, DEB together.

**Step 5.** From each of these equal sums subtract the common angle AED. By CN3, the remainders are equal: angle CEA is equal to angle DEB.

**Step 6.** Similarly, the straight line CE stands upon the straight line AB and makes with it the adjacent angles AEC and CEB, which by 1.13 are together equal to two right angles. But the angles AEC and AED were shown in Step 2 to be together equal to two right angles. By P4 two right angles are the same magnitude in both cases, so by CN1 the angles AEC, CEB together are equal to the angles AEC, AED together.

**Step 7.** From each of these equal sums subtract the common angle AEC. By CN3, the remainders are equal: angle CEB is equal to angle AED.

**Step 8.** Therefore angle AEC equals angle DEB and angle CEB equals angle AED, which are the two pairs of vertical angles. Hence, if two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be any triangle, and let one of its sides, BC, be produced beyond C to a point D [P2]. It is to be shown that the exterior angle ACD is greater than each of the interior and opposite angles BAC and ABC.

**Step 2.** Bisect AC at the point E [1.10], so that AE is equal to EC.

**Step 3.** Join BE [P1], and produce BE in a straight line beyond E to a point F [P2]; from the produced line cut off EF equal to BE [1.3]. Join FC [P1].

**Step 4.** In the triangles AEB and CEF, the side AE is equal to the side CE (Step 2), and the side EB is equal to the side EF (Step 3). Moreover, the straight lines AC and BF cut one another at E, so the vertical angles AEB and CEF are equal to one another [1.15].

**Step 5.** Therefore the two sides AE, EB are equal to the two sides CE, EF respectively, and the angles contained by the equal straight lines, namely AEB and CEF, are equal. Hence the base AB is equal to the base CF, the triangle AEB is equal to the triangle CEF, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles, those which the equal sides subtend [1.4]. In particular the angle EAB, subtended by EB, is equal to the angle ECF, subtended by EF; that is, the angle BAC is equal to the angle ECF.

**Step 6.** Since E lies between A and C, and B and F lie on opposite sides of E along the straight line BF, the point F falls on the side of AC remote from B and on the same side of BD as A; thus the straight line CF falls within the angle ECD, and the angle ECF is a part of the angle ECD, which is the same angle as ACD. Therefore the angle ACD is greater than the angle ECF [CN5].

**Step 7.** But the angle ECF is equal to the angle BAC (Step 5). Therefore the angle ACD is greater than the angle BAC.

**Step 8.** Next, produce AC beyond C to a point G [P2]. Bisect BC at the point H [1.10], so that BH is equal to HC. Join AH [P1], produce AH in a straight line beyond H to a point K [P2], cut off HK equal to AH [1.3], and join KC [P1].

**Step 9.** In the triangles AHB and KHC, the side BH is equal to the side CH (Step 8), the side AH is equal to the side KH (Step 8), and the vertical angles AHB and KHC, made by the straight lines BC and AK cutting one another at H, are equal to one another [1.15]. Therefore the two sides BH, HA are equal to the two sides CH, HK respectively, and the contained angles are equal; hence the base AB is equal to the base KC, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles which the equal sides subtend [1.4]. In particular the angle ABH, subtended by HA, is equal to the angle KCH, subtended by HK; that is, the angle ABC is equal to the angle KCB.

**Step 10.** Since H lies between B and C, and A and K lie on opposite sides of H along the straight line AK, the point K falls on the side of BC remote from A and on the same side of AG as B; thus the straight line CK falls within the angle BCG, and the angle KCB is a part of the angle BCG. Therefore the angle BCG is greater than the angle KCB [CN5], and hence the angle BCG is greater than the angle ABC (Step 9).

**Step 11.** But the straight lines AG and BD cut one another at C, so the vertical angles BCG and ACD are equal to one another [1.15]. Therefore the angle ACD is also greater than the angle ABC.

**Step 12.** Hence the exterior angle ACD is greater than each of the interior and opposite angles BAC and ABC. Since the triangle and the side produced were taken arbitrarily, in any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be any triangle. I say that two angles of the triangle ABC taken together in any manner are less than two right angles.

**Step 2.** Let the side BC be produced beyond C to a point D. [P2]

**Step 3.** Since the side BC of the triangle ABC has been produced to D, the angle ACD is the exterior angle at C, and it is therefore greater than each of the interior and opposite angles, namely greater than the angle ABC and greater than the angle CAB. [1.16]

**Step 4.** Let the angle ACB be added to each. Then, since the angle ACD is greater than the angle ABC, the angles ACD, ACB taken together are greater than the angles ABC, BCA taken together.

**Step 5.** But the straight line AC is set up on the straight line BD at the point C, making the adjacent angles ACD, ACB; therefore the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles. [1.13]

**Step 6.** Therefore the angles ABC, BCA taken together are less than two right angles.

**Step 7.** Again, since the angle ACD is also greater than the angle CAB (Step 3), let the angle ACB be added to each; then the angles ACD, ACB together are greater than the angles CAB, ACB together. But the angles ACD, ACB are equal to two right angles (Step 5). Therefore the angles CAB, ACB taken together are less than two right angles.

**Step 8.** Similarly, let the side AB be produced beyond B to a point F. [P2] Then the exterior angle CBF is greater than the interior and opposite angle CAB. [1.16] Let the angle ABC be added to each; then the angles CBF, ABC together are greater than the angles CAB, ABC together. But the straight line CB set up on the straight line AF makes the adjacent angles CBF, ABC equal to two right angles. [1.13] Therefore the angles CAB, ABC taken together are less than two right angles.

**Step 9.** Therefore in the triangle ABC every pair of angles, namely ABC with BCA, BCA with CAB, and CAB with ABC, is less than two right angles. Hence in any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In any triangle the greater side subtends the greater angle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle having the side AC greater than the side AB. It is to be proved that the angle ABC, which the greater side AC subtends, is greater than the angle BCA, which the lesser side AB subtends.

**Step 2.** Since AC is greater than AB, cut off from the greater AC a straight line AD equal to the lesser AB [1.3]. Because AD is equal to AB and AB is less than AC, AD is less than AC; therefore the point D falls on the side AC between A and C.

**Step 3.** Join BD [P1]. Since D lies on the side AC between A and C, the straight line BD falls within the angle ABC, so that the angle ABD is a part of the angle ABC; and since A, D, C lie in one straight line, the angle ADB is an exterior angle of the triangle BDC, formed by producing the side CD to A.

**Step 4.** In the triangle ABD the two sides AB and AD are equal to one another; therefore the angles at its base BD are equal, that is, the angle ABD is equal to the angle ADB [1.5].

**Step 5.** In the triangle BDC the side CD has been produced to A, so the exterior angle ADB is greater than the interior and opposite angle DCB [1.16]. But the angle DCB is the same as the angle ACB, since D lies on AC. Hence the angle ADB is greater than the angle ACB.

**Step 6.** The angle ABD is equal to the angle ADB (Step 4), and the angle ADB is greater than the angle ACB (Step 5); therefore the angle ABD is greater than the angle ACB.

**Step 7.** The angle ABC is the whole and the angle ABD is a part of it (Step 3); therefore the angle ABC is greater than the angle ABD [CN5].

**Step 8.** Since the angle ABC is greater than the angle ABD, and the angle ABD is greater than the angle ACB, the angle ABC is greater than the angle ACB. Thus the greater side AC subtends the greater angle ABC, while the lesser side AB subtends the lesser angle ACB. Therefore in any triangle the greater side subtends the greater angle. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 1.3, P1, 1.5, 1.16, CN5

result.statement: In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC greater than the angle BCA. I say that the side AC is also greater than the side AB.

**Step 2.** For, if not, AC is either equal to AB or less than it.

**Step 3.** Now AC is not equal to AB; for if it were, triangle ABC would be isosceles with AB equal to AC, and then the angle ABC would be equal to the angle ACB, since in isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another [1.5]. But by hypothesis the angle ABC is not equal to the angle ACB; therefore AC is not equal to AB.

**Step 4.** Neither is AC less than AB; for if it were, AB would be the greater side, and then the angle ACB (which AB subtends) would be greater than the angle ABC (which AC subtends), since in any triangle the greater side subtends the greater angle [1.18]; that is, the angle ABC would be less than the angle ACB. But by hypothesis the angle ABC is greater than the angle ACB, not less; therefore AC is not less than AB.

**Step 5.** And it was proved in Step 3 that AC is not equal to AB either. Therefore AC is neither equal to nor less than AB; hence AC is greater than AB.

**Step 6.** Therefore in any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one.
result.proof:
**Statement:** In any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle. It is to be shown that any two sides taken together are greater than the remaining side: that BA + AC > BC, that AB + BC > CA, and that BC + CA > AB.

**Step 2.** Produce the side BA beyond A in a straight line to a point D (P2), and on the produced part cut off AD equal to AC (1.3). Then D, A, B lie in one straight line with A between D and B.

**Step 3.** Join DC (P1). We now have the triangle DBC, and within it the triangle ADC.

**Step 4.** In triangle ADC, since DA = AC, the angles at the base DC are equal: angle ADC = angle ACD (1.5).

**Step 5.** The point A lies on the straight line DB between D and B, so the straight line CA falls within the angle BCD and divides it into the two angles BCA and ACD. Hence angle ACD is a part of angle BCD, and the whole is greater than the part: angle BCD > angle ACD (CN5).

**Step 6.** From Step 4 and Step 5, angle BCD > angle ADC, that is, angle BCD > angle BDC, since the angle ADC is the same as the angle BDC of triangle DBC.

**Step 7.** In triangle DBC the angle BCD is greater than the angle BDC. The greater angle is subtended by the greater side (1.19). The angle BCD is subtended by the side DB, and the angle BDC is subtended by the side BC; therefore DB > BC.

**Step 8.** Since D, A, B lie in a straight line with A between D and B, the straight line DB is made up of DA and AB together. Now DA = AC (Step 2); adding the same AB to each, DA + AB = AC + AB (CN2). Therefore DB = BA + AC.

**Step 9.** From Step 7 and Step 8, BA + AC > BC.

**Step 10.** In the same way, producing CB beyond B and cutting off a segment equal to BA, one shows that AB + BC > CA; and producing AC beyond C and cutting off a segment equal to CB, one shows that BC + CA > AB.

**Step 11.** Therefore in any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, P2, CN2, CN5, 1.3, 1.5, 1.19

result.statement: If on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed will be less than the remaining two sides of the triangle, but will contain a greaterangle.
result.proof:
## Proposition 1.21
**Statement:** If on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed will be less than the remaining two sides of the triangle, but will contain a greater angle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and on BC, one of its sides, from its extremities B and C, let the two straight lines BD, DC be constructed meeting within the triangle at the point D. I say that BD, DC are together less than the remaining two sides BA, AC of the triangle, but contain an angle BDC greater than the angle BAC.

**Step 2.** Produce BD in a straight line beyond D [P2]. Since D lies within the triangle ABC, the straight line BD produced through D passes out of the triangle across the side AC; let it meet AC at the point E. Thus B, D, E lie in one straight line with D between B and E, and E lies on AC between A and C.

**Step 3.** In the triangle ABE, the two sides AB, AE taken together are greater than the remaining side BE [1.20].

**Step 4.** Let EC be added to each. Then AB, AE, EC together are greater than BE, EC together [CN2]. But AE, EC together make up the whole side AC, since E lies on AC. Therefore BA, AC together are greater than BE, EC together.

**Step 5.** Again, in the triangle CED, the two sides CE, ED taken together are greater than the remaining side CD [1.20].

**Step 6.** Let DB be added to each. Then CE, ED, DB together are greater than CD, DB together [CN2]. But ED, DB together make up the whole straight line EB, since D lies on BE. Therefore CE, EB together are greater than CD, DB together.

**Step 7.** But BA, AC were proved greater than BE, EC (Step 4), and BE, EC are greater than BD, DC (Step 6). Therefore BA, AC are much greater than BD, DC; that is, the constructed straight lines BD, DC are less than the remaining two sides BA, AC of the triangle. This proves the first part.

**Step 8.** Next, in the triangle CDE the side ED has been produced to B; therefore the exterior angle BDC is greater than the interior and opposite angle CED [1.16].

**Step 9.** For the same reason, in the triangle ABE the side AE has been produced to C; therefore the exterior angle CEB is greater than the interior and opposite angle BAE, that is, the angle BAC [1.16].

**Step 10.** But the angle CED is the same angle as the angle CEB. Hence the angle BDC is greater than the angle CEB (Step 8), and the angle CEB is greater than the angle BAC (Step 9). Therefore the angle BDC is much greater than the angle BAC.

**Step 11.** Therefore, if on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed are less than the remaining two sides of the triangle, but contain a greater angle. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P2, CN2, 1.16, 1.20

result.statement: Out of three straight lines, which are equal to three given straight lines, to construct a triangle: thus it is necessary that two of the straight lines taken together in any manner should be greater than the remaining one.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A, B, C be the three given straight lines, and let any two of them taken together be greater than the remaining one: A and B together greater than C, A and C together greater than B, and B and C together greater than A. This condition is necessary, for in any triangle two sides taken together in any manner are greater than the remaining one (1.20); hence a triangle with sides equal to A, B, C can exist only if A, B, C satisfy it.

**Step 2.** Set out a straight line DE, terminated at D (P1), and produced indefinitely in the direction of E (P2), so that DE exceeds any of the given lines.

**Step 3.** On DE cut off DF equal to A, then FG equal to B, then GH equal to C (1.3), so that D, F, G, H lie in order on the straight line DE.

**Step 4.** With centre F and distance FD describe the circle DKL (P3).

**Step 5.** With centre G and distance GH describe the circle KLH (P3).

**Step 6.** The two circles cut one another. For the circle about F has radius FD equal to A, the circle about G has radius GH equal to C, and their centres are distant FG equal to B; since A and C together exceed B, the two circles reach one another, and since neither A nor C exceeds the sum of B and the other, neither circle lies wholly within the other; hence they meet at some point K. Join KF and KG (P1).

**Step 7.** Since the point F is the centre of the circle DKL, FD is equal to FK (D1.15). But FD is equal to A (Step 3); therefore KF is also equal to A (CN1).

**Step 8.** Since the point G is the centre of the circle KLH, GH is equal to GK (D1.15). But GH is equal to C (Step 3); therefore KG is also equal to C (CN1).

**Step 9.** And FG is equal to B by construction (Step 3).

**Step 10.** Therefore the three straight lines KF, FG, GK are equal to the three given straight lines A, B, C respectively; and the triangle KFG has been constructed out of three straight lines KF, FG, GK which are equal to the three given straight lines A, B, C. Q.E.F.

result.statement: On a given straight line and at a point on it to construct a rectilineal angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.
result.proof:
## Proposition 1.23
**Statement:** On a given straight line and at a point on it to construct a rectilineal angle equal to a given rectilineal angle.

Let AB be the given straight line, A the given point on it, and DCE the given rectilineal angle, contained by the straight lines CD and CE. It is required to construct on AB, at the point A, a rectilineal angle equal to the angle DCE.

**Step 1.** On the straight lines CD and CE take points D and E respectively, at random, and join the straight line DE [P1]. Then CDE is a triangle whose three sides are CD, DE, and EC.

**Step 2.** Since CD, DE, and EC are the three sides of the triangle CDE, any two of them taken together are greater than the remaining one [1.20]. Hence these three straight lines satisfy the condition required for constructing a triangle out of three straight lines equal to them.

**Step 3.** Out of three straight lines equal to CD, CE, and DE, construct on the straight line AB, at the point A, the triangle AFG, so that AF lies along AB and AF is equal to CD, AG is equal to CE, and FG is equal to DE [1.22].

**Step 4.** Consider the two triangles DCE and FAG. The two sides DC and CE are equal to the two sides FA and AG respectively, by construction, and the base DE is equal to the base FG, also by construction. Therefore the angles contained by the equal straight lines are equal, namely the angle DCE is equal to the angle FAG [1.8].

**Step 5.** Therefore on the given straight line AB, and at the point A on it, the rectilineal angle FAG has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal angle DCE. This is what was required to do.

**USED:** P1, 1.8, 1.20, 1.22

result.statement: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other, they will also have the base greater than the base.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and let the angle BAC be greater than the angle EDF; we must show that the base BC is greater than the base EF. Of the two sides AB, AC let AB be the one that is not greater than the other (if AB were greater than AC we would interchange the letters B, C and correspondingly E, F, which changes neither hypothesis nor conclusion). Since DE = AB and DF = AC, it follows that DE is not greater than DF.

**Step 2.** On the straight line DE, at the point D on it, construct the angle EDG equal to the angle BAC [1.23], taking G on the same side of DE as F. Cut off DG equal to AC [1.3], and join EG and FG [P1]. Since DG = AC and DF = AC, DG = DF [CN1].

**Step 3.** In the triangles BAC and EDG, the two sides AB, AC are equal to the two sides DE, DG respectively, and the contained angle BAC is equal to the contained angle EDG. Therefore the base BC is equal to the base EG [1.4].

**Step 4.** Since the angle EDG equals the angle BAC, which is greater than the angle EDF, and F and G lie on the same side of DE, the straight line DF falls within the angle EDG. Hence DF, produced if necessary, meets the straight line EG at a point K lying between E and G.

**Step 5.** Since DE is not greater than DG, the angle DGE is not greater than the angle DEG: if DE = DG the two angles are equal [1.5], and if DE < DG the greater side DG subtends the greater angle, so that angle DEG > angle DGE [1.18]. Moreover, in the triangle DEK the side EK is produced to G, so the exterior angle DKG is greater than the interior and opposite angle DEK, that is, angle DKG > angle DEG [1.16]. Hence angle DKG > angle DGK. In the triangle DKG the greater angle is subtended by the greater side, so DG > DK [1.19]. Since DG = DF, we have DF > DK; and as K and F lie on the same straight line drawn from D, the point K lies between D and F.

**Step 6.** Since K lies between D and F, the straight line GK falls within the angle DGF; therefore the angle DGF is greater than the angle DGK [CN5], and since K lies on GE, angle DGK is the angle EGF; thus angle DGF > angle EGF. Again, since K lies between E and G, the straight line FK falls within the angle EFG; therefore the angle EFG is greater than the angle KFG [CN5], and since K lies on FD, angle KFG is the angle DFG; thus angle EFG > angle DFG.

**Step 7.** Since DF = DG, the angle DFG is equal to the angle DGF [1.5]. Therefore angle EFG > angle DFG = angle DGF > angle EGF, so that the angle EFG is greater than the angle EGF.

**Step 8.** In the triangle EFG the greater angle EFG is subtended by the greater side, so EG > EF [1.19]. But EG = BC by Step 3. Therefore BC is greater than EF. Q.E.D.

Path note: the route chosen is the direct one (construct the larger angle on DE, compare EF with EG inside the isosceles triangle DFG, then apply 1.19). The choice of labelling in Step 1 and the argument of Step 5 are included so that the position of F beyond EG, on which Steps 6 and 7 depend, is established rather than read from the figure.

result.statement: If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the base greater than the base, they will also have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and let the base BC be greater than the base EF. I say that the angle BAC is also greater than the angle EDF.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the angle BAC is not greater than the angle EDF. Then the angle BAC is either equal to the angle EDF or less than it; these are the only remaining possibilities, and we show that each leads to a contradiction.

**Step 3.** First, suppose the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF. Then the two triangles ABC, DEF have the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, and the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, namely the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF. Therefore, by 1.4, the base BC is equal to the base EF.

**Step 4.** But by hypothesis the base BC is greater than the base EF, so BC is not equal to EF. This contradicts Step 3. Therefore the angle BAC is not equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 5.** Next, suppose the angle BAC is less than the angle EDF. Then the two triangles DEF, ABC have the two sides DE, DF equal to the two sides AB, AC respectively, but the angle EDF contained by the equal straight lines DE, DF is greater than the angle BAC contained by the equal straight lines AB, AC. Therefore, by 1.24, the base EF is greater than the base BC; that is, BC is less than EF.

**Step 6.** But by hypothesis the base BC is greater than the base EF, so BC is not less than EF. This contradicts Step 5. Therefore the angle BAC is not less than the angle EDF.

**Step 7.** By Steps 4 and 6, the angle BAC is neither equal to nor less than the angle EDF. Since the two angles must stand in one of the three relations of greater, equal, or less, the angle BAC is greater than the angle EDF.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the base greater than the base, they will also have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 1.4, 1.24

result.statement: If two triangles have the two angles equal to two angles respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely, either the side adjoining the equal angles, or that subtending one of the equal angles, they will also have the remaining sides equal tothe remaining sides and the remaining angle to the remaining angle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two angles DEF, EFD respectively, namely the angle ABC to the angle DEF and the angle BCA to the angle EFD; and let them also have one side equal to one side. We treat first the case in which the side adjoining the equal angles is given equal, namely BC equal to EF, and afterwards the case in which the side subtending one of the equal angles is given equal, namely AB equal to DE. In each case we show that the remaining sides are equal to the remaining sides, AB to DE and AC to DF (or BC to EF and AC to DF), and the remaining angle BAC equal to the remaining angle EDF.

**Step 2.** Case 1: let BC be equal to EF. I say that AB is equal to DE. For, if AB is unequal to DE, one of them is greater. Let AB be the greater. From BA, the greater, cut off BG equal to DE, the less [1.3], and join GC [P1].

**Step 3.** Then, since BG is equal to DE and BC is equal to EF, the two sides GB, BC are equal to the two sides DE, EF respectively; and the angle GBC is equal to the angle DEF, since G lies on BA and the angle ABC was assumed equal to the angle DEF. Therefore the base GC is equal to the base DF, the triangle GBC is equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles, those which the equal sides subtend; in particular the angle GCB is equal to the angle DFE [1.4].

**Step 4.** But the angle DFE is by hypothesis equal to the angle BCA. Therefore the angle GCB is also equal to the angle BCA [CN1]. But the angle GCB is a part of the angle BCA, since G lies on BA between B and A; hence the less is equal to the greater, which is impossible [CN5]. Therefore AB is not unequal to DE; that is, AB is equal to DE.

**Step 5.** Now, since AB is equal to DE and BC is equal to EF, the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DE, EF respectively, and the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF. Therefore the base AC is equal to the base DF, and the remaining angle BAC is equal to the remaining angle EDF [1.4]. This completes Case 1.

**Step 6.** Case 2: let the side subtending one of the equal angles be given equal, namely AB equal to DE (AB subtends the angle BCA and DE subtends the equal angle EFD). I say that BC is equal to EF. For, if BC is unequal to EF, one of them is greater. Let BC be the greater. From BC, the greater, cut off BH equal to EF, the less [1.3], and join AH [P1].

**Step 7.** Then, since BH is equal to EF and AB is equal to DE, the two sides AB, BH are equal to the two sides DE, EF respectively; and the angle ABH is equal to the angle DEF, since H lies on BC and the angle ABC was assumed equal to the angle DEF. Therefore the base AH is equal to the base DF, the triangle ABH is equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles, those which the equal sides subtend; in particular the angle BHA is equal to the angle EFD [1.4].

**Step 8.** But the angle EFD is by hypothesis equal to the angle BCA. Therefore the angle BHA is equal to the angle BCA, that is, to the angle HCA [CN1].

**Step 9.** But in the triangle AHC the side CH has been produced to B, so that the angle BHA is an exterior angle of the triangle AHC; therefore the angle BHA is greater than the interior and opposite angle HCA [1.16]. Thus the angle BHA is both equal to and greater than the angle HCA, which is impossible. Therefore BC is not unequal to EF; that is, BC is equal to EF.

**Step 10.** Now, since AB is equal to DE and BC is equal to EF, the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DE, EF respectively, and the angle ABC is equal to the angle DEF. Therefore the base AC is equal to the base DF, and the remaining angle BAC is equal to the remaining angle EDF [1.4]. This completes Case 2.

**Step 11.** Therefore, in both cases, if two triangles have the two angles equal to two angles respectively and one side equal to one side, whether the side adjoining the equal angles or that subtending one of the equal angles, they also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides and the remaining angle equal to the remaining angle. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the alternate angles equal to one another, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line EF, falling on the two straight lines AB and CD, make the alternate angles AEF and EFD equal to one another, where E lies on AB and F lies on CD, and A, C are on one side of EF while B, D are on the other side. I say that AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for contradiction, that AB and CD are not parallel. Since the two straight lines lie in the same plane (the straight line EF meets both of them), by D1.23 they must, when produced indefinitely, meet one another in some direction: either in the direction of B and D, or in the direction of A and C.

**Step 3.** First suppose that AB and CD, when produced (P2), meet in the direction of B and D at a point G. Then EF, EG, and FG are three straight lines forming the triangle GEF.

**Step 4.** In triangle GEF, the side GE is produced beyond E to A (since A, E, G lie on the one straight line AB with E between A and G). Hence the angle AEF is an exterior angle of triangle GEF at the vertex E, and the angle EFG is one of the interior and opposite angles.

**Step 5.** By 1.16, the exterior angle AEF is greater than the interior and opposite angle EFG.

**Step 6.** But the angle EFG is the same angle as the angle EFD, since F, D, G lie on the one straight line CD with D between F and G (or G beyond D on the same side of F). Therefore the angle AEF is greater than the angle EFD.

**Step 7.** This contradicts the hypothesis that the angle AEF is equal to the angle EFD. Therefore AB and CD, when produced, do not meet in the direction of B and D.

**Step 8.** Next suppose that AB and CD, when produced (P2), meet in the direction of A and C at a point H. Then EF, EH, and FH form the triangle HEF.

**Step 9.** In triangle HEF, the side HF is produced beyond F to D (since H, F, D lie on the one straight line CD with F between H and D). Hence the angle EFD is an exterior angle of triangle HEF at the vertex F, and the angle HEF is one of the interior and opposite angles.

**Step 10.** By 1.16, the exterior angle EFD is greater than the interior and opposite angle HEF. But the angle HEF is the same angle as the angle AEF, since H lies on EA produced. Therefore the angle EFD is greater than the angle AEF.

**Step 11.** This again contradicts the hypothesis that the angle AEF is equal to the angle EFD. Therefore AB and CD, when produced, do not meet in the direction of A and C either.

**Step 12.** Thus AB and CD, being in the same plane and being produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet one another in either direction. By D1.23, such straight lines are parallel. Therefore AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 13.** Therefore, if a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the straight lines are parallel to one another. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P2, 1.16, D1.23

result.statement: If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line EF fall on the two straight lines AB, CD, cutting AB at G and CD at H, and let it make either (i) the exterior angle EGB equal to the interior and opposite angle GHD on the same side, or (ii) the interior angles on the same side, namely BGH and GHD, together equal to two right angles. I say that in either case AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 2.** [Case (i)] Suppose the angle EGB is equal to the angle GHD. Since the straight lines AB and EF cut one another at G, the vertical angles EGB and AGH are equal to one another [1.15].

**Step 3.** But the angle EGB is equal to the angle GHD by hypothesis. Therefore the angle AGH is also equal to the angle GHD, since things equal to the same thing are equal to one another [CN1].

**Step 4.** The angles AGH and GHD are the alternate angles made by the straight line EF falling on AB and CD. Since these alternate angles are equal, AB is parallel to CD [1.27].

**Step 5.** [Case (ii)] Now suppose the angles BGH and GHD together are equal to two right angles. Since the straight line GH is set up on the straight line AB at G, the adjacent angles AGH and BGH together are equal to two right angles [1.13].

**Step 6.** Since all right angles are equal to one another [P4], the two right angles to which AGH, BGH are equal and the two right angles to which BGH, GHD are equal are the same magnitude; therefore the angles AGH, BGH together are equal to the angles BGH, GHD together [CN1].

**Step 7.** Let the angle BGH be subtracted from each. Then the remaining angle AGH is equal to the remaining angle GHD [CN3].

**Step 8.** The angles AGH and GHD are the alternate angles made by EF falling on AB and CD, and they have been shown equal. Therefore AB is parallel to CD [1.27].

**Step 9.** Hence, whether the exterior angle is equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side are equal to two right angles, the straight lines AB, CD are parallel to one another. Q.E.D.

result.statement: A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.
result.proof:
**Statement:** A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.

Let AB and CD be parallel straight lines, and let the straight line EF fall on them, cutting AB at G and CD at H, with E on the side of AB remote from CD and F on the side of CD remote from AB. I say that (i) the alternate angles AGH and GHD are equal, (ii) the exterior angle EGB is equal to the interior and opposite angle GHD, and (iii) the interior angles on the same side, BGH and GHD, are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 1.** Suppose the angle AGH is not equal to the angle GHD. Then one of them is greater; let the angle AGH be the greater.

**Step 2.** Add the angle BGH to each. Then the angles AGH, BGH together are greater than the angles BGH, GHD together.

**Step 3.** Since the straight line GH stands on the straight line AB at G, the angles AGH, BGH together are equal to two right angles [1.13]. Therefore the angles BGH, GHD together are less than two right angles.

**Step 4.** Thus the straight line EF, falling on the two straight lines AB and CD, makes the interior angles on the same side, BGH and GHD, together less than two right angles; therefore AB and CD, if produced indefinitely, meet on the side of B and D [P5].

**Step 5.** But AB and CD, being parallel, do not meet however far they are produced in either direction [D1.23]. This is impossible; so the angle AGH is not greater than the angle GHD. If instead the angle GHD were the greater, adding the angle GHC to each would give the angles GHD, GHC together greater than the angles GHC, AGH together; since the angles GHD, GHC together are equal to two right angles [1.13], the angles AGH, GHC together would be less than two right angles, so that AB and CD would meet on the side of A and C [P5], which is again impossible [D1.23]. Therefore neither angle is greater, and the angle AGH is equal to the angle GHD. This proves (i).

**Step 6.** Since the straight lines AB and EF cut one another at G, the vertical angles AGH and EGB are equal [1.15]. But the angle AGH is equal to the angle GHD (Step 5); therefore the angle EGB is equal to the angle GHD [CN1]. This proves (ii).

**Step 7.** Add the angle BGH to each. Then the angles EGB, BGH together are equal to the angles BGH, GHD together [CN2].

**Step 8.** Since the straight line GB stands on the straight line EF at G, the angles EGB, BGH together are equal to two right angles [1.13]. Therefore the angles BGH, GHD together are also equal to two right angles [CN1]. This proves (iii).

Therefore a straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.

**USED:** P5, CN1, CN2, D1.23, 1.13, 1.15

result.statement: Straight lines parallel to the same straight line are also parallel to one another.
result.proof:
## Proposition 1.30
**Statement:** Straight lines parallel to the same straight line are also parallel to one another.

**Step 1.** Let each of the straight lines AB, CD be parallel to the straight line EF. I say that AB is also parallel to CD.

**Step 2.** Let a straight line be drawn falling upon the three straight lines AB, EF, CD [P1], and let it meet AB at G, EF at H, and CD at K. Of the three points G, H, K on this straight line, either H lies between G and K, or it does not; in the latter case, since AB and CD enter the hypothesis in exactly the same way, we may interchange their names if necessary so that G lies between H and K. We treat these two cases in turn.

**Step 3.** First let H lie between G and K. Since the straight line GK falls upon the parallel straight lines AB, EF, the alternate angles AGK and GHF are equal to one another [1.29].

**Step 4.** Again, since the straight line GK falls upon the parallel straight lines EF, CD, the exterior angle GHF is equal to the interior and opposite angle GKD [1.29].

**Step 5.** Therefore each of the angles AGK, GKD is equal to the angle GHF; hence the angle AGK is equal to the angle GKD [CN1].

**Step 6.** But the angles AGK, GKD are the alternate angles made by the straight line GK falling upon the two straight lines AB, CD. Therefore AB is parallel to CD [1.27].

**Step 7.** Next let G lie between H and K. Since the straight line HK falls upon the parallel straight lines EF, AB, the exterior angle KGA is equal to the interior and opposite angle GHE [1.29].

**Step 8.** Again, since the straight line HK falls upon the parallel straight lines EF, CD, the alternate angles EHK and HKD are equal to one another [1.29]. And since G lies on the straight line HK, the angle EHK is the same angle as the angle GHE, and the angle HKD is the same angle as the angle GKD; so the angle GHE is equal to the angle GKD.

**Step 9.** Therefore each of the angles AGK, GKD is equal to the angle GHE; hence the angle AGK is equal to the angle GKD [CN1]. These are again the alternate angles made by the straight line GK falling upon the two straight lines AB, CD; therefore AB is parallel to CD [1.27].

**Step 10.** Thus in either case AB is parallel to CD. Therefore straight lines parallel to the same straight line are also parallel to one another. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, 1.29, CN1, 1.27

result.statement: Through a given point to draw a straight line parallel to a given straight line.
result.proof:
## Proposition 1.31
**Statement:** Through a given point to draw a straight line parallel to a given straight line.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given point and BC the given straight line. Take a point D at random on BC, and join the straight line AD [P1].

**Step 2.** On the straight line DA, and at the point A on it, construct the angle DAE equal to the angle ADC, placing E on the side of AD opposite to C, so that the angles EAD and ADC lie on alternate sides of AD [1.23].

**Step 3.** Produce the straight line EA in a straight line to F, so that EAF is one straight line passing through A [P2].

**Step 4.** The straight line AD, falling on the two straight lines BC and EF, makes the alternate angles EAD and ADC equal to one another (Step 2).

**Step 5.** Therefore EAF is parallel to BC [1.27].

**Step 6.** Hence through the given point A the straight line EAF has been drawn parallel to the given straight line BC. Q.E.F.

**USED:** P1, P2, 1.23, 1.27

result.statement: In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles, and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles.
result.proof:
## Proposition 1.32
**Statement:** In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles, and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and let one of its sides, BC, be produced to D [P2].

**Step 2.** Through the point C let CE be drawn parallel to the straight line AB [1.31].

**Step 3.** Since AB is parallel to CE, and the straight line AC falls upon them, the alternate angles BAC and ACE are equal to one another [1.29].

**Step 4.** Again, since AB is parallel to CE, and the straight line BD falls upon them, the exterior angle ECD is equal to the interior and opposite angle ABC [1.29].

**Step 5.** The angle ACE was shown equal to the angle BAC (Step 3), and the angle ECD equal to the angle ABC (Step 4). Therefore the whole angle ACD, which is made up of the angles ACE and ECD, is equal to the two interior and opposite angles BAC and ABC taken together [CN2]. This proves the first part of the proposition.

**Step 6.** Let the angle ACB be added to each. Then the angles ACD and ACB taken together are equal to the three angles ABC, BCA, CAB taken together [CN2].

**Step 7.** But the straight line AC stands upon the straight line BD at the point C, making the adjacent angles ACD and ACB; therefore the angles ACD and ACB are equal to two right angles [1.13].

**Step 8.** Therefore the three angles ABC, BCA, CAB are also equal to two right angles [CN1].

**Step 9.** Hence, in any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles (Step 5), and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles (Step 8). Q.E.D.

**USED:** P2, 1.31, 1.29, CN2, 1.13, CN1

result.statement: The straight lines joining equal and parallel straight lines (at the extremities which are) in the same directions (respectively) are themselves also equal and parallel.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB and CD be equal and parallel straight lines, and let the straight lines AC and BD join them at the extremities which are in the same directions, so that A corresponds to C and B corresponds to D. It is required to prove that AC and BD are equal and parallel.

**Step 2.** Join BC. [P1]

**Step 3.** Since AB is parallel to CD, and the straight line BC falls upon them, the alternate angles ABC and BCD are equal to one another. [1.29]

**Step 4.** Now in the triangles ABC and DCB, the side AB is equal to the side DC (by hypothesis), and the side BC is common to both; hence the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively. Moreover the contained angle ABC is equal to the contained angle DCB (Step 3).

**Step 5.** Therefore the base AC is equal to the base BD, the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend; in particular the angle ACB, subtended by AB, is equal to the angle CBD, subtended by DC. [1.4]

**Step 6.** Since the straight line BC, falling on the two straight lines AC and BD, makes the alternate angles ACB and CBD equal to one another (Step 5), the straight line AC is parallel to the straight line BD. [1.27]

**Step 7.** And AC was also proved equal to BD (Step 5). Therefore the straight lines AC and BD, which join the equal and parallel straight lines AB and CD at the extremities in the same directions, are themselves also equal and parallel. Q.E.D.

result.statement: In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas.
result.proof:
**Statement:** In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas.

**Step 1.** Let ACDB be a parallelogrammic area, so that AB is parallel to CD and AC is parallel to BD, and let BC be its diameter, the straight line joined from B to C [P1]. It is to be proved that AB = CD, AC = BD, angle BAC = angle CDB, angle ABD = angle ACD, and that BC bisects the area ACDB.

**Step 2.** Since AB is parallel to CD, and the straight line BC has fallen upon them, the alternate angles ABC and BCD are equal to one another [1.29].

**Step 3.** Since AC is parallel to BD, and the straight line BC has fallen upon them, the alternate angles ACB and CBD are equal to one another [1.29].

**Step 4.** Therefore ABC and DCB are two triangles having the two angles ABC, BCA equal to the two angles DCB, CBD respectively, and one side equal to one side, namely the side BC which is common to both and adjoins the equal angles. Hence they also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides respectively and the remaining angle to the remaining angle: AB = DC, AC = DB, and angle BAC = angle CDB [1.26].

**Step 5.** Since angle ABC = angle BCD (Step 2) and angle CBD = angle ACB (Step 3), adding equals to equals, the whole angle ABD (= ABC + CBD) is equal to the whole angle ACD (= BCD + ACB) [CN2].

**Step 6.** Also angle BAC = angle CDB (Step 4). Therefore in the parallelogrammic area ACDB the opposite sides AB, CD and AC, BD are equal, and the opposite angles BAC, CDB and ABD, ACD are equal to one another.

**Step 7.** It remains to show that the diameter bisects the area. Since AB = DC (Step 4), BC is common, and the angle ABC contained by the sides AB, BC is equal to the angle BCD contained by the sides DC, CB (Step 2), the two sides AB, BC are equal to the two sides DC, CB respectively and the contained angles are equal; therefore the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DCB [1.4].

**Step 8.** Therefore the diameter BC bisects the parallelogrammic area ACDB, which together with Step 6 is what was to be proved.

**USED:** P1, 1.29, 1.26, CN2, 1.4

result.statement: Parallelograms which are on the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another.
result.proof:
## Proposition 1.35
**Statement:** Parallelograms which are on the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD and EBCF be parallelograms on the same base BC and in the same parallels AF and BC, so that the points A, D, E, F all lie on the straight line AF. Take first the configuration in which D lies between A and E, and let the sides EB and DC cut one another at the point G.

**Step 2.** Since ABCD is a parallelogram, its opposite sides are equal, so AD = BC [1.34]. Likewise, since EBCF is a parallelogram, EF = BC [1.34].

**Step 3.** Since AD and EF are each equal to BC, AD = EF [CN1].

**Step 4.** Let DE be added to each. Then the whole AE is equal to the whole DF [CN2].

**Step 5.** Again, since ABCD is a parallelogram, its opposite sides AB and DC are equal, so AB = DC [1.34].

**Step 6.** Since AB is parallel to DC (they are opposite sides of the parallelogram ABCD) and the straight line AF falls on them, the exterior angle FDC is equal to the interior and opposite angle EAB [1.29].

**Step 7.** Therefore in the triangles EAB and FDC, the two sides EA, AB are equal to the two sides FD, DC respectively (Steps 4 and 5), and the angle EAB contained by them is equal to the angle FDC (Step 6). Hence the base EB is equal to the base FC, and the triangle EAB is equal to the triangle FDC [1.4].

**Step 8.** Let the triangle DGE be subtracted from each of the equal triangles EAB and FDC. Then the remaining trapezium ABGD is equal to the remaining trapezium EGCF [CN3].

**Step 9.** Let the triangle GBC be added to each of these equal trapezia. Then the whole parallelogram ABCD is equal to the whole parallelogram EBCF [CN2].

**Step 10.** The remaining configurations reduce to the same argument. If E lies between A and D, then in place of Step 4 the common segment ED is subtracted from the equals AD and EF, giving AE = DF [CN3], and Steps 5 to 9 proceed unchanged with the roles of the subtracted and added triangles determined by the figure.
